mitigation_mechanism: The evidence points to a small reduction in flood impact, with no size given. Wooded riparian strips act on the water pathway rather than on the crop: they slow the flow of water from the land into receiving water bodies by increasing infiltration, reducing flow velocity and providing temporary storage [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_1], and mature woodland is the more effective form because of its structural complexity and the deadwood it delivers to the watercourse [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2]. The only field finding runs from removal: in Marqués de Comillas, Chiapas, floods along with the seasonal drying of permanent streams and altered river dynamics were associated with the loss of riparian forest [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. A European model of strips of willow, poplar or grass planted along watercourses rates the chance of reducing recurring floods as high or very high in about 1/7 to 1/5 of the landscapes where buffers are set up [ev_flood_hazard_englund21_8].
caveats: Nothing here is a measured reduction in flood damage to a farm. The Chiapas finding describes what losing riparian forest was associated with, in a case study, not what establishing a buffer delivers [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. The European estimate is a model, and in most landscapes it does not rate the flood benefit as high [ev_flood_hazard_englund21_8]. The review that states the benefit confines it to moderate flooding and makes it depend on the extent, location, age and density of the woodland, with mature woodland more effective [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2], which a new strip is not. No source reports a buffer holding up in a severe or extreme flood. The effect works on water moving into streams and rivers, so the farm giving up land need not be where the benefit lands. mitigation_mechanism: Both findings describe what standing riparian vegetation was already doing, and infer the mechanism from the cost of its removal. In Marques de Comillas, Chiapas, floods, the seasonal drying up of permanent streams and alterations in river dynamics have been associated with the loss of riparian forests [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. The implied mechanism is retention and conveyance of flood water in a vegetated headwater floodplain.
caveats: Neither source measured what a restored buffer does: both are framed on vegetation loss, and the Mexican finding is an association recorded in a case study, not an attributed effect [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. No magnitude, return period or flood severity is reported, so nothing can be said about behaviour in a severe or extreme flood — a practice that slows ordinary runoff is not thereby a defence against an extreme event. The benefit described sits downstream of the restored reach [ev_flood_hazard_osbo93_19], which separates who bears the land-use cost from who gains. The pool is a US review of a temperate high-income floodplain and a tropical upper-middle-income case study; no low- or lower-middle-income evidence supports this row.
